topic: Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act 2026

subtopics.title: Passage and timeline
subtopics.summary: The United States enacted the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 after House passage and Senate approval. The House voted 262 to 159 on 16 September, and the President signed the Act into law on 18 September 2026. The measure matters for India because India remains one of the major buyers of Russian crude.
facts: House of Representatives passed the legislation 262-159 on 16 Sep
The legislation followed Senate approval
Presidential signing into law on 18 Sep 2026
Act aims primarily at increasing economic pressure on Russia over the Ukraine War
Act also extends and strengthens certain sanctions against Iran
India is significant because it remains one of the major buyers of Russian crude

subtopics.title: Key provisions
subtopics.summary: The Act authorises tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas, a substantial reduction from the 500% original proposal. It also authorises tariffs of up to 500% on Russian-origin goods, subject to specified exceptions. A 180-day review cycle for relevant purchasers and defined conditions for ending the sanctions framework complete its core design.
facts: Tariffs of up to 100% on the 5 largest purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas
100% ceiling is a substantial reduction from the original 500% proposal

Framework may be affected if Russia signs an accepted peace agreement, ceases military hostilities and ends activities undermining the Ukrainian Government

subtopics.title: Legal permanence and US trade tools
subtopics.summary: The earlier 25% punitive tariff on India was based on an Executive Order, and in February 2026 the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the broader tariff regime that included it. The new measure has been passed by Congress, signed and converted into federal law, which gives it greater legal permanence. A presidential waiver under the Act requires formal justification to Congress.

subtopics.title: Global and India implications
subtopics.summary: The measure illustrates growing use of secondary sanctions and tariff instruments to influence the behaviour of third countries. It could change global oil trade patterns as major buyers diversify suppliers and reconfigure energy contracts. For India, Russia is the top oil supplier, so potential tariffs complicate bilateral trade while India balances strategic autonomy with its energy interests.

quizzes.passage:
The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 is a law that the United States has enacted. The measure followed Senate approval and House passage, and it was then signed by the President. Its main aim is to increase economic pressure on Russia, and it also extends and strengthens certain sanctions against Iran. The Act targets political, financial, energy and commercial networks linked to Russia's war in Ukraine. It is now federal law with greater legal permanence.

The Act's criteria bring major buyers of Russian oil and gas within its scope. India is one such buyer because it remains one of the major buyers of Russian crude. Tariffs under the Act can fall on the largest purchasers of Russian energy and on facilitators of Russian oil sanctions evasion. Certain goods of Russian origin may also face tariffs, subject to specified exceptions.

The list of relevant purchasers is not fixed. It is reviewed periodically, in consultation with other senior officials. Countries that import only a small share of their natural gas from Russia can qualify for an exception if they take significant steps to reduce such imports. The sanctions framework may also be affected if certain conditions relating to the war are met.

quizzes.passage:
The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 was enacted by the United States in September 2026. The Act is aimed mainly at economic pressure on Russia over the war in Ukraine, and it also strengthens certain sanctions against Iran. Its criteria place major buyers of Russian energy within its scope. The measure was passed by Congress and signed into federal law, which gives it greater legal permanence. It follows an earlier punitive tariff on India for buying Russian oil. The authorisation covers tariffs on major purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas.

India remains one of the major buyers of Russian crude, so the measure matters for India's energy planning. Russia is a major source of India's oil, and the country depends on imports to meet a large part of its energy demand. This makes the measure significant for India.

The measure reflects a broader pattern in which tariffs and sanctions are used to shape the conduct of other countries. Crude oil is traded in a connected global market.

Russia's war in Ukraine remains the central context for the measure. Indian policymakers face a difficult set of choices. They must weigh their relationships with the United States, Russia and other major powers while protecting national energy interests.
